records.s1A_reason:
二、为什么这轮触发 Step 1A
核心问题很明确：
题干已经明确写了，患者**“one month ago, I was diagnosed with coronary heart disease”，说明她在这次就诊前已经有过一次医疗接触/检查**。
但模型在现病史里写的是：
“she has not sought medical attention until now.” 
这属于你量表里的：
Step 1A 红线 1：与题干明确事实冲突。
 不是模糊推断，而是和已知事实正面打架。
records.s1B_reason:
除了上面的硬冲突，这轮还有多处高风险越界：
 写成 “The discomfort is intermittent”，题干未明确间断发作； 
 写成 “The symptoms have not been associated with specific triggers”，题干没有给出； 
 写成 “She denies any acute worsening of symptoms, syncope, palpitations, or radiation”，这些阴性信息题干未提供； 
 写成 “good medication adherence”，题干也没有明确给出依从性结论； 
 在管理部分又写 “This is an inpatient admission” 作为前提假设，虽然题目角色是住院接诊助手，但这不是病历事实本身。 
这符合量表里的：
推理性阴性 / 细节补写
模板化阴性补写
事实层、判断层、待补层混写
records.s2_1_r:
这项我给低分，原因很硬。
虽然它抓到了不少主轴信息：
 63岁女性； 
 心前区胸闷近1月； 
 不痛； 
 休息后可缓解； 
 伴反酸、气促、手脚乏力； 
 既往糖尿病、高血压、甲状腺结节手术史、青霉素过敏。 
但关键问题是它已经出现明确事实冲突，而且还叠加了多处补写：
 “直到现在才就医”与题干冲突； 
 “间断发作”未给； 
 “无明确诱因”被改写成“无特定触发因素”； 
 “否认急性加重/晕厥/心悸/放射痛”均未给； 
 “依从性良好”未给。 
所以这项只能给 3 分。
records.s2_2_r:
这轮的问题比第二轮更明显。
 它不是完全没有分层意识，但在病历文书化部分已经把大量未确认内容写成事实，再在后文继续拿这些内容当依据推进诊断。
 这会直接破坏文本边界，让读者分不清：
 哪些是病人确实说过的； 
 哪些是模型推断的； 
 哪些其实应该回到追问区。 
所以这项也只能给 3 分。
records.s2_3_r:
单看形式，这一轮还是规整的：
 主诉简洁； 
 HPI、Past History、缺失信息、诊断分析、下一步动作分块清楚； 
 医学语言自然。 
这说明它会写。
 但这项主要看“结构化整理与语言转译”，不等于事实边界没问题。
 所以我给 8 分，不再往上。
records.s2_4_r:
这部分它的主方向没有完全跑偏：
 仍然把心源性问题放在前面； 
 仍然把 UA / NSTE-ACS 放进必须先排除； 
 也考虑了 GERD、焦虑、糖尿病自主神经病变、贫血等鉴别。 
但它的问题在于：
 把 “possibly representing stable exertional angina” 提得过早； 
 证据里又写 “improves with rest suggests exertional angina pattern”，这一步跨得太大； 
 因为题干并未明确“劳力诱发”这一关键前提。 
所以方向基本对，但分层强度和定性时点仍不够克制，给 6 分。
records.s2_5_r:
它能搭出一个像样的闭环：
 当前最可能方向； 
 需要先排除的高危诊断； 
 证据与证据不足； 
 后续检查与管理。 
但闭环的问题在于：
 它部分建立在“补写出来的事实”之上。
 因此这不是一个边界干净的闭环，只能给 6 分。
records.s3_1_r:
这部分整体不差，它抓到了不少真正影响判断的缺口：
 一个⽉前“冠心病”到底如何诊断； 
 ECG； 
 当前是否有标准抗缺血/抗血小板/调脂治疗； 
 糖尿病和血压控制情况； 
 运动耐量； 
 反酸与胸闷的关系； 
 既往超声心动图等。 
但仍有漏项，比如：
 每次胸闷持续多久； 
 是否平卧加重、夜间发作； 
 是否伴出汗、濒死感； 
 是否有近一周模式变化。
 所以不是满分。
records.s3_2_r:
它分了 high / medium / low priority，说明有优先级意识。
 但排序还不够锋利：
在当前胸闷首诊场景下，症状模式本身（静息还是劳力、持续多久、是否进展）和 ECG 应是最顶层；
 而它把“既往冠心病资料”“当前 GDMT 状态”等也提得很靠前，说明它更像在做“心血管规范化评估”，而不是最贴近首诊现场的轻重缓急排序。
records.s3_3_r:
大部分追问是有判别力的：
 既往冠脉解剖会改变当前风险级别； 
 ECG 会改变急性缺血判断； 
 运动耐量能改变 stable vs unstable 的判断； 
 反酸与胸闷的时间关系会改变 GERD 的排位。 
所以这项给 8 分是合适的。
records.s4_1_r:
这版工作流是能落地的，尤其是：
 先补 ECG； 
 再 serial troponin； 
 再看既往 CAD 资料； 
 再做实验室、超声、后续应激评估。 
顺序总体比“检查大礼包式输出”更接近真实接诊。
 但它的问题是把不少住院/专科优化动作也拉得比较前，且建立在“这是住院收治、已在监护流程中”的假设上，现实感略打折。
records.s4_2_r:
它有一定教学价值，比如：
 提醒单次 troponin 阴性不能排掉 UA； 
 提醒需要 ECG； 
 提醒慢病管理和 GDMT 不应忽视。 
但它对年轻医生最大的风险恰恰在于：
它写得很像，但边界不干净。
 新手很容易把它补写进去的“无特定诱因”“否认放射痛”“依从性良好”也当成已经问到的事实。
 因此带教价值有，但防错价值不够高。

records.prompt:
Patient information: Female, Age: 63  

Patient’s self-report:  
Doctor, I feel uncomfortable in this area of my chest (precordial region), it feels tight but not painful. It has been almost a month. Sometimes I also have acid reflux and feel short of breath, but I have not coughed or vomited. Resting for a while helps relieve it. My hands and feet feel weak. One month ago, I was diagnosed with coronary heart disease. I also have diabetes and hypertension and have been taking medications continuously. One medication is called “metoprolol tartrate tablets,” 25 mg each time, half a tablet in the morning. Another is called “gliquidone tablets,” 30 mg each time, one tablet three times a day (morning, noon, and evening). I have been taking them for eight years and have felt fine. I usually don’t pay much attention to these conditions. Ten years ago, I had surgery for thyroid nodules. By the way, doctor, please do not prescribe penicillin for me—I am allergic to it.  

I do not smoke or drink. My own health and my family’s health are generally good, with no known hereditary diseases. Since this discomfort started, my appetite and sleep have been acceptable, bowel and bladder habits are normal, and my weight has not changed much. However, because of the chest tightness, I feel very anxious and worried something might go wrong, so my mental state is not very good.  

Physical examination:  
T: 36.4°C  P: 70 bpm  R: 22 breaths/min  BP: 130/80 mmHg  
Clear consciousness, listless mental state, normal development, moderate nutrition. Skin and mucous membranes without jaundice, no petechiae or ecchymosis, no palpable superficial lymph node enlargement. Head without deformity, pupils equal, round, and reactive to light, no cyanosis of lips, tongue midline. Neck soft, no jugular venous distension, trachea midline, no thyroid enlargement bilaterally. Chest without deformity, breath sounds clear in both lungs, no dry or moist rales. Cardiac findings detailed in specialist examination. Abdomen flat and soft, no abdominal wall varicosities, no visible peristaltic waves, no tenderness or rebound tenderness, liver and spleen not palpable below costal margin, no obvious masses, shifting dullness negative, bowel sounds 4–6 times/min. No pitting edema in both lower limbs. Limb muscle strength and tone normal, physiological reflexes present, no pathological signs elicited.  

Specialist examination:  
BP: 130/80 mmHg  
No jugular venous distension, hepatojugular reflux negative. No abnormal bulging or depression in the precordial area. Apical impulse located 1.0 cm medial to the left midclavicular line at the 5th intercostal space. No cardiac enlargement. Heart rate 70 bpm, regular rhythm. No murmurs or pericardial friction rubs heard in any valve areas. Peripheral vascular signs negative.  

Laboratory and instrumental examinations:  
At this hospital:  
Myocardial infarction panel:  
Troponin I (TnI): <0.01 ng/ml  
Creatine kinase-MB (CK-MB): <2.50 ng/ml  
Myoglobin (Myo): <30.0 ng/ml  
Procalcitonin (PCT): 0.13 ng/ml ↑  

You are an inpatient admission assistant for a young doctor. Based on the following patient information, complete the initial admission summary and preliminary assessment.  

Please output according to the following structure:  

Part 1: Medical Record Documentation  
Please organize the patient information into the following three sections:  

Chief complaint  
[Within 20 words, including the main symptom and duration.]  

History of present illness  
[Describe the current illness in chronological order, focusing on the main complaint of this visit, including onset time, triggers, nature, persistence or intermittence, severity, relationship with activity/food/position, impact on activity, associated symptoms, relieving factors, tests performed and results, medications used and their effects. Also describe changes in mental state, sleep, appetite, bowel and bladder habits, weight, and physical strength since onset as much as possible. Only use information provided in the prompt; do not add unprovided details.]  

Past medical history  
[Based on the given information, summarize the patient’s past health status, chronic disease history, surgical/trauma history, allergy history, personal history, and family history.  
Record known information truthfully. If not provided, mark as “not provided” or list under information to be further inquired. Do not mechanically apply negative templates.  
Disease or medication names reported by others should be placed in quotation marks.]  

Requirements:  
Convert colloquial expressions into standardized medical language  
Use only information provided in the prompt  
Do not add unprovided information  
Do not mechanically apply negative templates  
Place disease or medication names reported by others in quotation marks  

Part 2: Identification of Key Missing Information  
List information that still needs to be asked under “high priority / medium priority / low priority,” and for each item explain:  
Why it needs to be asked now  
Which aspect it mainly affects: risk stratification / diagnostic ranking / next-step examination  
How different answers might change the current assessment  

Part 3: Preliminary Diagnosis and Analysis  
Based on the patient’s history, physical examination, specialist examination, and auxiliary tests, complete the following:  

Most likely current diagnostic direction  
Dangerous diagnoses that must be ruled out first  
Other common differential diagnoses to consider  

For each, list diagnostic evidence and specify which information comes from medical history, physical examination, or auxiliary tests  
Explain areas where current evidence is insufficient  

Next-step examination and management recommendations  
Must include at least:  
Current primary risk stratification actions  
Priority recommended examinations  
Whether monitoring / consultation / further evaluation is needed  
Conclusions or treatments that should not be made prematurely  

Please follow the clinical workflow rules below while completing the task:  
Diagnostic priority: Always prioritize ruling out life-threatening diseases before differentiating common conditions.  
Special population recognition: Elderly patients and those with multiple comorbidities often present atypically and may have masked symptoms; maintain high vigilance to avoid missed diagnoses.  
Symptom stratification: Strictly distinguish main symptoms from associated symptoms; use main symptoms to localize etiology and associated symptoms to aid differentiation.  
Standardized inquiry: Include both positive symptoms and key negative symptoms relevant to differential diagnosis; for prolonged courses, focus on disease progression and factors of aggravation/relief.  
Purposeful questioning: Each follow-up question should have a clear goal—rule out high-risk diseases, narrow differential diagnosis, or support confirmation—avoid purposeless questioning.  
Evidence-based diagnosis: All diagnoses must be supported by objective evidence; when information is incomplete, clearly state existing evidence and gaps.  
External information caution: Do not directly accept patient-reported external diagnoses; rely only on objective reports and medical records.  
Critical differential thinking: Establish a complete differential diagnosis list and exclude step by step using symptoms, signs, and tests to form a closed-loop reasoning process without subjective assumptions.  
Preliminary diagnosis ranking: List diagnoses directly related to the chief complaint first, followed by underlying diseases and comorbidities.  
Test selection logic: Follow “urgent before non-urgent, simple before complex”; prioritize key tests that ensure safety, avoid indiscriminate comprehensive or expensive testing.  
Holistic treatment thinking: Treatment should consider not only the current illness but also overall condition, comorbidities, allergy history, and treatment tolerance to formulate an individualized plan.
records.output:
---

Part 1: Medical Record Documentation


Chief complaint


Precordial tightness for nearly one month.

History of present illness


The patient is a 63-year-old female presenting with precordial tightness that began approximately one month ago. The discomfort is described as tightness without pain. The symptom is intermittent and is sometimes accompanied by acid reflux and shortness of breath. No cough or vomiting has occurred. The tightness is relieved by rest. The patient also reports weakness in both hands and feet. One month ago, the patient was diagnosed with "coronary heart disease" at an outside facility. Since symptom onset, the patient reports increased anxiety and worry about potential cardiac complications, resulting in poor mental state. Appetite and sleep have remained acceptable. Bowel and bladder habits are normal. Weight has been stable.

Past medical history


Chronic disease history: The patient has a history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension, both managed with medications for eight years. The patient reports taking "metoprolol tartrate tablets" 12.5 mg once daily in the morning and "gliquidone tablets" 30 mg three times daily (morning, noon, evening) with good tolerance. One month ago, the patient was diagnosed with "coronary heart disease" at an outside facility; details of diagnostic workup and specific findings are not provided.

Surgical/trauma history: Ten years ago, the patient underwent surgery for thyroid nodules. Specific surgical details and pathology results are not provided.

Allergy history: Penicillin allergy.

Personal history: The patient denies tobacco use and alcohol consumption.

Family history: Family health is generally good with no known hereditary diseases.

Information to be further inquired:

- Details of the "coronary heart disease" diagnosis one month ago (diagnostic tests performed, coronary anatomy if known, revascularization status)

- Specific antihypertensive and antiplatelet/anticoagulant medications beyond metoprolol

- Diabetes control status (hemoglobin A1c, home glucose monitoring results)

- Blood pressure control at home

- Thyroid function status and current thyroid medication use

- Lipid management and statin therapy

- Previous cardiac testing (stress tests, echocardiography, coronary angiography)

---

Part 2: Identification of Key Missing Information


High priority


1. Details of recent "coronary heart disease" diagnosis

- Why needed: Essential to determine whether the patient has known obstructive coronary artery disease, prior myocardial infarction, or prior revascularization (percutaneous coronary intervention or coronary artery bypass grafting).

- Affects: Risk stratification and diagnostic ranking. If the patient has known severe coronary disease or recent stenting, current symptoms may represent in-stent restenosis, stent thrombosis, or progression of disease requiring urgent evaluation.

- Impact on assessment: Known multivessel disease or left main disease would elevate risk substantially and lower threshold for invasive evaluation. Prior normal coronary angiography would shift probability toward noncardiac causes.

2. Complete medication list, particularly antiplatelet therapy and statin

- Why needed: Patients with established coronary disease should be on guideline-directed medical therapy including aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor (if recent acute coronary syndrome or percutaneous coronary intervention), high-intensity statin, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker.

- Affects: Risk stratification and next-step management. Absence of appropriate secondary prevention medications suggests either the "coronary heart disease" diagnosis was not confirmed or represents a significant treatment gap.

- Impact on assessment: If the patient is not on antiplatelet therapy or statin despite documented coronary disease, this represents both a diagnostic uncertainty and a treatment priority.

3. Relationship of symptoms to exertion

- Why needed: The patient reports that rest relieves symptoms, but it is unclear whether exertion consistently provokes symptoms or whether symptoms occur at rest.

- Affects: Diagnostic ranking between stable angina and unstable angina/acute coronary syndrome. Symptoms at rest or with minimal exertion suggest higher-risk unstable angina.

- Impact on assessment: If symptoms occur only with significant exertion and are consistently relieved by rest, this favors stable angina. If symptoms occur at rest or with progressively less exertion over the past month, this suggests unstable angina requiring urgent evaluation.

4. Hemoglobin A1c and recent glucose control

- Why needed: Diabetic patients, particularly those with poor glycemic control, have higher cardiovascular risk and may present with atypical symptoms.

- Affects: Risk stratification and assessment for diabetic autonomic neuropathy, which can cause atypical anginal presentations.

- Impact on assessment: Poor glycemic control increases likelihood of progressive coronary disease and microvascular complications.

5. Thyroid function status

- Why needed: The patient has a history of thyroid nodule surgery ten years ago. Hypothyroidism can cause fatigue, weakness, and dyspnea. Hyperthyroidism can cause palpitations, dyspnea, and anxiety.

- Affects: Diagnostic ranking. Thyroid dysfunction is a reversible cause of symptoms and can also exacerbate cardiac conditions.

- Impact on assessment: Uncontrolled hyperthyroidism could precipitate angina or atrial arrhythmias. Hypothyroidism could contribute to fatigue and weakness.

Medium priority


6. Timing and characteristics of acid reflux symptoms

- Why needed: To determine whether acid reflux occurs concurrently with chest tightness or independently, and whether it is meal-related.

- Affects: Diagnostic ranking between gastroesophageal reflux disease and cardiac ischemia.

- Impact on assessment: If reflux symptoms are temporally associated with chest tightness and occur after meals or when supine, gastroesophageal reflux disease becomes more likely. If reflux is independent of chest tightness, both conditions may coexist.

7. Characteristics of weakness in hands and feet

- Why needed: To determine whether weakness is subjective fatigue, objective motor weakness, or sensory symptoms (paresthesias).

- Affects: Differential diagnosis. True motor weakness could suggest neurologic disease, diabetic neuropathy, or electrolyte abnormalities. Generalized fatigue could be cardiac, endocrine, or related to anxiety.

- Impact on assessment: Objective motor weakness would require neurologic evaluation. Generalized fatigue is nonspecific but consistent with cardiac or metabolic etiologies.

8. Previous echocardiography results

- Why needed: To assess baseline left ventricular function, valvular disease, and pulmonary pressures.

- Affects: Risk stratification and next-step examination. Reduced ejection fraction or significant valvular disease would elevate risk.

- Impact on assessment: Normal left ventricular function would be reassuring. Reduced function or regional wall motion abnormalities would suggest prior infarction or ongoing ischemia.

9. Home blood pressure measurements

- Why needed: To assess adequacy of blood pressure control beyond single office measurement.

- Affects: Risk stratification and treatment optimization. Uncontrolled hypertension is a modifiable risk factor.

- Impact on assessment: Persistently elevated blood pressure would require medication adjustment and contributes to cardiovascular risk.

Low priority


10. Family history details

- Why needed: To identify premature coronary disease in first-degree relatives, which increases patient risk.

- Affects: Long-term risk stratification.

- Impact on assessment: Positive family history would support more aggressive preventive measures but does not change acute management.

11. Dietary habits and exercise tolerance

- Why needed: To assess functional capacity and lifestyle factors.

- Affects: Risk stratification and rehabilitation planning.

- Impact on assessment: Poor functional capacity would suggest need for cardiac rehabilitation. Dietary assessment informs diabetes and lipid management.

12. Sleep quality and symptoms of sleep apnea

- Why needed: Obstructive sleep apnea is common in patients with obesity, hypertension, and coronary disease.

- Affects: Long-term risk modification.

- Impact on assessment: Untreated sleep apnea contributes to hypertension and cardiovascular risk but does not change acute evaluation.

---

Part 3: Preliminary Diagnosis and Analysis


Most likely current diagnostic direction


Stable angina pectoris in the setting of known coronary artery disease

Diagnostic evidence:

- Medical history: One-month duration of precordial tightness relieved by rest is consistent with stable angina. The patient has established risk factors including age 63, female sex, diabetes mellitus, and hypertension, all of which increase pretest probability of coronary artery disease. Recent diagnosis of "coronary heart disease" suggests known coronary disease, though details are lacking.[1][2][3]

- Physical examination: Vital signs are stable with blood pressure 130/80 mmHg and heart rate 70 bpm. No signs of acute decompensation such as jugular venous distension, pulmonary rales, or peripheral edema. Cardiac examination shows no murmurs or gallops.

- Auxiliary tests: Troponin I, creatine kinase-MB, and myoglobin are all negative, effectively ruling out acute myocardial infarction. The negative cardiac biomarkers in the setting of one-month symptom duration make acute coronary syndrome unlikely.[2][4]

Areas where evidence is insufficient:

- Lack of details regarding the recent "coronary heart disease" diagnosis (coronary anatomy, severity of stenosis, revascularization status)

- Unclear whether symptoms are consistently exertional or occur at rest

- No objective assessment of ischemia (stress testing, coronary computed tomographic angiography, or invasive angiography results not provided)

- No echocardiography to assess left ventricular function or regional wall motion abnormalities

- No electrocardiogram provided to assess for ischemic changes, prior infarction, or conduction abnormalities

Dangerous diagnoses that must be ruled out first


1. Unstable angina / non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome

Diagnostic evidence:

- Medical history: One-month duration with intermittent symptoms could represent crescendo angina if symptoms are worsening in frequency or severity. Diabetes and female sex are associated with atypical presentations of acute coronary syndrome.[1][2][5]

- Physical examination: Hemodynamically stable with no signs of acute heart failure.

- Auxiliary tests: Negative troponin effectively rules out myocardial infarction but does not exclude unstable angina. Procalcitonin is mildly elevated at 0.13 ng/ml, which is nonspecific.[4]

Areas where evidence is insufficient:

- No electrocardiogram provided to assess for ST-segment or T-wave changes

- Unclear whether symptoms are progressive (worsening frequency, duration, or occurring with less exertion)

- No serial troponin measurements to confirm sustained negative trend

- No risk score calculation (HEART score, EDACS) to quantify 30-day major adverse cardiac event risk[4]

2. Pulmonary embolism

Diagnostic evidence:

- Medical history: Shortness of breath is present, which could be consistent with pulmonary embolism. However, the one-month duration and intermittent nature are less typical for acute pulmonary embolism.

- Physical examination: Respiratory rate is 22 breaths/min, which is at the upper limit of normal. No tachycardia (heart rate 70 bpm). Clear breath sounds bilaterally with no evidence of pleural effusion or consolidation.

- Auxiliary tests: No D-dimer measurement performed. Negative troponin does not exclude pulmonary embolism.

Areas where evidence is insufficient:

- No D-dimer measurement

- No assessment of pulmonary embolism risk factors (recent immobilization, surgery, malignancy, prior venous thromboembolism)

- No chest imaging (chest radiograph or computed tomographic pulmonary angiography)

- Clinical presentation (one-month duration, relief with rest) is atypical for acute pulmonary embolism

3. Acute aortic syndrome (aortic dissection)

Diagnostic evidence:

- Medical history: The patient has hypertension, a major risk factor for aortic dissection. However, the symptom is described as tightness rather than sudden-onset severe or "ripping" pain, which is more characteristic of dissection.[6][1]

- Physical examination: Blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg without evidence of pulse differential or blood pressure differential between limbs. No neurologic deficits. Peripheral vascular signs are negative.

- Auxiliary tests: Negative troponin is consistent with aortic dissection if coronary involvement has not occurred. No D-dimer measurement, which has high sensitivity for acute aortic syndrome.[6]

Areas where evidence is insufficient:

- No D-dimer measurement (high sensitivity for acute aortic syndrome; negative D-dimer effectively rules out dissection in low-risk patients)[6]

- No chest radiograph to assess for mediastinal widening

- No computed tomographic angiography of the aorta

- Clinical presentation (gradual onset, one-month duration, relief with rest) is highly atypical for acute aortic dissection

Other common differential diagnoses to consider


1. Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)

Diagnostic evidence:

- Medical history: The patient explicitly reports acid reflux symptoms occurring concurrently with chest tightness. Gastroesophageal reflux disease can cause retrosternal discomfort that mimics cardiac ischemia.[1][7]

- Physical examination: Abdomen is soft and nontender without masses.

- Auxiliary tests: No specific testing for gastroesophageal reflux disease performed.

Areas where evidence is insufficient:

- Unclear whether symptoms are meal-related or positional (worse when supine)

- No trial of proton pump inhibitor therapy to assess symptomatic response

- No upper endoscopy or esophageal pH monitoring

2. Anxiety disorder with somatic symptoms

Diagnostic evidence:

- Medical history: The patient reports significant anxiety and worry about cardiac complications, resulting in poor mental state. Anxiety can manifest as chest tightness, dyspnea, and weakness.[1]

- Physical examination: Patient appears listless but otherwise normal examination.

- Auxiliary tests: Negative cardiac biomarkers support absence of acute cardiac injury.

Areas where evidence is insufficient:

- No formal assessment of anxiety symptoms or panic disorder

- Symptoms preceded the anxiety (anxiety developed in response to symptoms), suggesting anxiety is secondary rather than primary cause

3. Diabetic autonomic neuropathy

Diagnostic evidence:

- Medical history: Eight-year history of diabetes mellitus. Diabetic autonomic neuropathy can cause atypical anginal presentations and exercise intolerance.[1]

- Physical examination: No orthostatic vital signs documented.

- Auxiliary tests: No hemoglobin A1c or assessment of glycemic control.

Areas where evidence is insufficient:

- No assessment of autonomic function

- No documentation of other autonomic symptoms (gastroparesis, orthostatic hypotension, resting tachycardia)

4. Microvascular angina (cardiac syndrome X)

Diagnostic evidence:

- Medical history: Female sex, diabetes, and hypertension are risk factors for microvascular dysfunction. Symptoms of chest tightness with exertion could represent microvascular angina.[3]

- Physical examination: Normal cardiac examination.

- Auxiliary tests: Negative troponin suggests no myocardial necrosis.

Areas where evidence is insufficient:

- Requires exclusion of obstructive coronary disease by coronary computed tomographic angiography or invasive angiography

- No stress testing to assess for inducible ischemia

- Diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out epicardial coronary disease

---

Next-step examination and management recommendations


Assumptions: The patient is presenting to an inpatient service, suggesting concern for potential acute coronary syndrome. The patient is hemodynamically stable. It is assumed that basic laboratory testing (complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, lipid panel, hemoglobin A1c) and electrocardiogram have been or will be obtained as part of standard admission workup but were not provided in the initial information.

Current primary risk stratification actions


Immediate (within hours):

- Obtain 12-lead electrocardiogram to assess for ST-segment changes, T-wave inversions, Q waves, or conduction abnormalities. Compare with prior electrocardiograms if available.[1]

- Repeat troponin measurement at 3 hours from initial measurement to confirm sustained negative trend and rule out delayed troponin rise.[4][1]

- Calculate HEART score using history, electrocardiogram, age, risk factors, and troponin to quantify 30-day major adverse cardiac event risk. A HEART score ≤3 with negative serial troponins identifies low-risk patients who may not require further inpatient cardiac testing.[4]

- Obtain chest radiograph to assess cardiac silhouette, pulmonary vasculature, and exclude alternative diagnoses (pneumonia, pneumothorax, pleural effusion, mediastinal widening).[8][6]

Priority recommended examinations


Within 24-48 hours:

- Transthoracic echocardiography to assess left ventricular systolic function, regional wall motion abnormalities, valvular disease, and pulmonary pressures. This is essential given the known "coronary heart disease" diagnosis.[3][1]

- Obtain records from outside facility regarding the recent "coronary heart disease" diagnosis, including any coronary angiography, stress testing, or coronary computed tomographic angiography results. This is critical to determine baseline coronary anatomy and guide further evaluation.

- Laboratory testing:

 - Hemoglobin A1c to assess glycemic control

 - Lipid panel (if not recently checked)

 - Thyroid-stimulating hormone and free T4 given history of thyroid surgery

 - D-dimer if clinical suspicion for pulmonary embolism or acute aortic syndrome remains after electrocardiogram and chest radiograph review[6]

 - Brain natriuretic peptide if concern for heart failure

If low-risk by HEART score and negative serial troponins:

- Outpatient stress testing (exercise stress echocardiography or pharmacologic stress myocardial perfusion imaging) or coronary computed tomographic angiography to assess for obstructive coronary disease and inducible ischemia. Choice depends on patient's ability to exercise, local expertise, and whether anatomic versus functional assessment is preferred. Coronary computed tomographic angiography has high sensitivity and negative predictive value for excluding obstructive disease.[9][3][10][1]

If intermediate-to-high risk by HEART score or concerning electrocardiogram findings:

- Inpatient stress testing or invasive coronary angiography depending on risk level and institutional protocols.[3][1]

Monitoring and consultation needs


- Continuous telemetry monitoring during initial evaluation to detect arrhythmias or ischemic electrocardiogram changes.

- Cardiology consultation is reasonable given known "coronary heart disease" diagnosis and persistent symptoms, particularly if stress testing or invasive evaluation is being considered.[3][1]

- Gastroenterology consultation may be considered if cardiac workup is unrevealing and gastroesophageal reflux disease remains a leading diagnosis. Empiric trial of proton pump inhibitor therapy is reasonable before consultation.[1][7]

Red flags requiring escalation


- New electrocardiogram changes (ST-segment elevation or depression, new T-wave inversions, new Q waves) → Urgent cardiology consultation and consideration for invasive coronary angiography

- Rising troponin on serial measurements → Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction; urgent cardiology consultation

- Hemodynamic instability (hypotension, tachycardia, respiratory distress) → Intensive care unit transfer and urgent evaluation for acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, or aortic dissection

- New murmur or signs of acute valvular regurgitation → Urgent echocardiography and cardiology consultation

- Symptoms at rest or with minimal exertion despite medical therapy → Consider urgent invasive evaluation

Conclusions or treatments that should not be made prematurely


- Do not discharge without objective cardiac testing (stress test or coronary computed tomographic angiography) unless the patient is clearly low-risk by validated risk score and has negative serial troponins with nonischemic electrocardiogram.[4][1]

- Do not attribute symptoms solely to anxiety or gastroesophageal reflux disease without first excluding cardiac ischemia in this high-risk patient with diabetes, hypertension, and known "coronary heart disease".[1][5]

- Do not initiate empiric antianginal therapy intensification (e.g., increasing beta-blocker, adding long-acting nitrate or calcium channel blocker) without first confirming the diagnosis of stable angina with objective testing.[3]

- Do not perform coronary angiography without first attempting noninvasive risk stratification unless the patient has high-risk features (ongoing chest pain, hemodynamic instability, electrocardiogram changes, rising troponin).[3][1]

---

Is there any additional information about the patient's recent "coronary heart disease" diagnosis, such as whether coronary angiography or stress testing was performed, or whether the symptoms have been progressively worsening over the past month?

records.s1A_reason:
Step 1A：未触发
这轮没有像前面某些轮次那样写出“ECG 正常”之类未提供却已完成且结果明确的事实，也没有把主线错误降到 GERD/焦虑，更没有给出明显不安全处理建议。虽然它写了“outside facility”“intermittent”等补写，但这些更接近 Step 1B 的边界问题，而不是 Step 1A 一票否决。
records.s1B_reason:
2）Step 1B：触发
这一轮的主要扣分点在于：
 把胸闷写成 intermittent，题干并未明确持续还是间断； 
 把“一个月前诊断冠心病”具体化成 at an outside facility，题干没给出“外院”信息； 
 把主方向直接写成 stable angina pectoris in the setting of known coronary artery disease，但它自己又承认“是否与运动稳定相关、是否静息发作、是否有客观缺血证据”都还不清楚； 
 在“Assumptions”里加入“患者正在住院流程、标准入院检查将会完成”等前提，虽然它标明是 assumption，但这会让事实层、判断层、待补层边界变得不够干净。
records.s2_1_r:
2.1 信息抽取准确性：6/10
优点是大部分核心事实抓得比较完整：
 主诉、病程、胸前区发闷不痛、休息后缓解、伴反酸和气促、手脚乏力、糖尿病/高血压/冠心病/甲状腺手术史、青霉素过敏、生活方式、情绪与睡眠食欲大小便体重变化，都有覆盖。 
但不能给高分，因为它还是有几处越界补写：
 “intermittent”； 
 “at an outside facility”； 
 “with good tolerance”虽然不算严重错，但比题干原始表述更主观。
 这些没有导致主线反转，但已经影响“事实忠实度”。
records.s2_2_r:
2.2 事实 / 判断 / 待补层分层清晰度：8/10
这一轮比前几轮好的一点，是它把
 事实整理， 
 缺失信息， 
 初步诊断， 
 evidence insufficient， 
 next steps
 分块写得比较清楚。 
扣分点在于：
 虽然框架上分层了，但在正文和诊断中仍然把“稳定型心绞痛倾向”写得偏实，说明边界控制仍不够克制。
records.s2_3_r:
2.3 首诊病历结构化整理与医学语言转译：8/10
整体结构清楚，可读性好，主诉规范，现病史顺序顺，既往史分类也比较规整。对年轻医生来说，这一版已经接近“能直接拿来当底稿修改”的水平。
没给 10 分，原因不是格式，而是转译中掺入了轻度推断，不算纯忠实转写。
records.s2_4_r:
2.4 初步诊断与风险分层合理性：8/10
这轮的主线是对的：
 把 stable angina / chronic CAD symptoms 放在最可能方向； 
 但同时把 unstable angina / NSTE-ACS 放在必须先排的危险诊断里； 
 也补充了 PE、主动脉夹层、GERD、焦虑、糖尿病自主神经病变、微血管性心绞痛等鉴别。 
问题在于，它还是把“稳定型心绞痛”定得稍快。
 因为题干没有明确：
 是否固定劳力诱发； 
 每次持续多久； 
 是否近来进行性加重； 
 是否静息也发作。
 所以这项给 8，不给 10。
records.s2_5_r:
2.5 诊断依据链与闭环合理性：8/10
这一轮的闭环算比较完整：
 有最可能方向； 
 有危险诊断优先排除； 
 有 evidence insufficient； 
 有下一步风险分层动作、优先检查、监测、会诊、红旗信号和避免过早结论。 
扣分点还是同一个：
 闭环虽然成立，但底座不够“干净”，因为主方向部分依赖了若干未确认前提。
records.s3_1_r:
3.1 关键缺失信息识别完整性：6/10
这轮提出了不少有价值的缺口：
 最近“冠心病”怎么诊断出来的； 
 目前用药全貌，尤其抗血小板和他汀； 
 症状与劳力关系； 
 糖控； 
 反酸性质； 
 手脚无力性质； 
 既往超声； 
 家庭血压等。 
但它有一个明显短板：
没有把 ECG 本身列进缺失信息清单的高优先级项。
 它在后面的诊断不足和 next steps 里提到了 ECG，但 Part 2 作为“关键缺口识别”时，漏掉这个点，在胸闷首诊题里是明显失分。再加上对“每次持续多久、是否进展、是否静息发作/夜间发作、是否放射、是否伴出汗心悸”等核心分层问题覆盖仍不够全，所以这项只能给 6 分。
records.s3_2_r:
3.2 首诊追问排序与分层意识：6/10
它有 high / medium / low priority，说明有排序意识。
 但优先级还不够锋利：
在这个胸闷场景里，最应该顶在最前面的其实是：
 症状模式细化； 
 ECG； 
 是否进展/静息发作； 
 既往 CAD 资料。 
而它把甲状腺功能放到 high priority，把 ECG 放丢在 Part 2 外面，这说明它的排序更像“完整内科评估”，还不是最贴近首诊安全分层的排序。
records.s3_3_r:
3.3 关键追问的信息增益与判别力：8/10
这一项相对不错。
 因为它追问的大多数问题确实会改变判断：
 既往冠脉解剖会改变当前风险层级； 
 目前是否有抗血小板/他汀会影响“已知 CAD 是否治疗不足”的理解； 
 劳力关系会改变 stable vs unstable 排序； 
 糖控会影响 atypical ischemia 的判断。 
所以它不是“为了问而问”，只是有价值问题的排序还不够极致。
records.s4_1_r:
4.1 下一步动作优先级与首诊工作流可执行性：8/10
这一轮工作流是能落地的：
 先 ECG； 
 再复查 troponin； 
 再做 HEART score； 
 同时做胸片； 
 再补外院资料、超声和实验室评估； 
 最后根据低危/中高危分流到门诊应激/CTA 或住院进一步评估。 
这比“直接甩一串检查清单”更接近真实流程。
 扣分点在于：
 它过度依赖“住院流程/HEART 评分/serial troponin”这套胸痛路径，略有指南化、急诊路径化； 
 对于“先补最关键几句病史再决定路径”这一点，强调还不够。
records.s4_2_r:
4.2 教学启发、风险提醒与年轻医生友好性：8/10
这部分其实写得不错：
 明确列出 red flags； 
 明确说不能过早归因于焦虑或 GERD； 
 明确说不能在没做客观缺血评估前就草率强化抗心绞痛治疗； 
 对年轻医生有一定“避坑”价值。 
它没到 10 分的原因，是它仍然没有很好地提醒年轻医生：
哪些是题干事实，哪些只是当前推测。
 如果边界提醒更强，它会更像示范答案。

---

Part 1: Medical Record Documentation


Chief Complaint


Precordial tightness for nearly one month.

History of Present Illness


The patient is a 63-year-old female who reports approximately one month of precordial tightness. The discomfort is described as tight but not painful. It is intermittent and relieved by rest. Associated symptoms include acid reflux and dyspnea, without cough or vomiting. The patient also reports generalized weakness in the hands and feet. One month ago, the patient was diagnosed with "coronary heart disease" at an outside facility. The patient has been experiencing significant anxiety and worry about her condition, resulting in poor mental state, though appetite, sleep, bowel and bladder function remain normal, and weight has been stable.

Past Medical History


Chronic Disease History:

- "Coronary heart disease" diagnosed one month ago at outside facility

- Diabetes mellitus, duration 8 years, treated with "gliquidone tablets" 30 mg three times daily

- Hypertension, duration 8 years, treated with "metoprolol tartrate tablets" 12.5 mg once daily in the morning

- The patient reports generally poor attention to these chronic conditions

Surgical/Trauma History:

- Thyroid nodule surgery 10 years ago

Allergy History:

- Penicillin allergy

Personal History:

- Denies tobacco use

- Denies alcohol use

Family History:

- Reports generally good family health

- No known hereditary diseases

---

Part 2: Identification of Key Missing Information


High Priority


1. Detailed characterization of chest discomfort pattern

- Why needed: To distinguish stable angina from unstable angina/ACS, which has critical management implications[1][2]

- Affects: Risk stratification and diagnostic ranking

- Impact: Unstable angina features (rest pain >20 minutes, crescendo pattern, new onset severe pain) would mandate urgent invasive evaluation, whereas stable exertional pattern supports outpatient workup[1][3]

2. Details of the external "coronary heart disease" diagnosis

- Why needed: To understand what diagnostic testing was performed and what the diagnosis is based on

- Affects: Next-step examination planning

- Impact: If based on angiography showing obstructive disease, management differs from diagnosis based on symptoms alone or non-obstructive disease[4]

3. Electrocardiogram (ECG) findings

- Why needed: Essential for detecting ischemic changes, prior infarction, or conduction abnormalities[5][6]

- Affects: Risk stratification and immediate management

- Impact: New ST-segment changes or T-wave inversions would elevate concern for ACS; baseline abnormalities (LVH, LBBB) complicate interpretation[5][6]

4. Relationship of symptoms to exertion, meals, and position

- Why needed: To differentiate cardiac ischemia from GERD and other causes[6][7]

- Affects: Diagnostic ranking

- Impact: Exertional provocation relieved by rest suggests angina; postprandial symptoms or relief with antacids suggests GERD; positional variation suggests musculoskeletal or pericardial causes[6]

5. Current medication regimen details

- Why needed: To assess adequacy of goal-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for chronic coronary disease[4]

- Affects: Next-step management

- Impact: Inadequate antiplatelet, statin, or anti-ischemic therapy would warrant optimization before pursuing invasive testing[4]

Medium Priority


6. Glycemic control status

- Why needed: Diabetes increases cardiovascular risk and may affect troponin interpretation[2][4]

- Affects: Risk stratification

- Impact: Poor control (HbA1c >7%) increases risk; diabetics may have chronically elevated troponin[2]

7. Blood pressure control pattern

- Why needed: Uncontrolled hypertension can cause type 2 MI and affects treatment decisions[5]

- Affects: Diagnostic ranking and management

- Impact: Severe hypertension (>180/110) could contribute to supply-demand mismatch

8. Functional capacity assessment

- Why needed: To determine ability to perform exercise stress testing and assess symptom severity[4]

- Affects: Next-step examination selection

- Impact: Inability to exercise necessitates pharmacologic stress testing; <5 METs suggests poor prognosis[8][6]

9. Depression and anxiety screening

- Why needed: Depression/anxiety are common in CAD patients, affect symptom perception, and worsen prognosis[9][10]

- Affects: Diagnostic ranking and comprehensive management

- Impact: Positive screening (PHQ-2/PHQ-9) would warrant treatment and may explain symptom burden[10]

Low Priority


10. Lipid profile and statin use

- Why needed: For comprehensive cardiovascular risk management[4]

- Affects: Long-term preventive therapy

- Impact: Guides statin intensity and LDL targets

11. Renal function

- Why needed: Affects medication dosing and troponin interpretation[2]

- Affects: Treatment selection

- Impact: Chronic kidney disease elevates baseline troponin and increases cardiovascular risk[2]

12. Details of thyroid surgery and current thyroid function

- Why needed: Thyroid dysfunction can affect cardiovascular symptoms

- Affects: Differential diagnosis

- Impact: Hyperthyroidism can cause tachycardia and angina; hypothyroidism affects metabolism

---

Part 3: Preliminary Diagnosis and Analysis


Most Likely Current Diagnostic Direction


Stable angina pectoris in the setting of known coronary artery disease

Supporting evidence:

- History: One-month duration of precordial tightness relieved by rest, recent diagnosis of "coronary heart disease," multiple cardiovascular risk factors (diabetes, hypertension, age 63, female)[1][4]

- Physical examination: Vital signs stable, no acute distress, no signs of heart failure (no JVD, no edema, clear lungs)[1]

- Laboratory: Negative cardiac biomarkers (troponin I, CK-MB, myoglobin all below detection limits) argue against acute myocardial injury[6]

Insufficient evidence:

- No ECG provided to assess for ischemic changes or prior infarction[6]

- Lack of details about exertional relationship and symptom duration per episode[1][6]

- No documentation of prior cardiac testing (stress test, angiography) to confirm obstructive CAD[4][11]

- Inadequate information about current antianginal and preventive medications[4]

Dangerous Diagnoses That Must Be Ruled Out First


1. Unstable angina / Non-ST elevation acute coronary syndrome

Supporting evidence:

- History: New-onset symptoms within past month, diabetes and hypertension increase ACS risk[1][2][3]

- Physical examination: Tachypnea (RR 22) could suggest cardiac decompensation, though other vital signs stable[5]

Against this diagnosis:

- History: Symptoms present for one month without progression, relieved by rest (not prolonged rest pain >20 minutes)[1]

- Laboratory: Negative troponin, CK-MB, and myoglobin argue strongly against acute myocardial injury[12][6]

- Physical examination: No signs of acute heart failure or hemodynamic instability[1]

Insufficient evidence:

- No ECG to assess for dynamic ST-T changes[1][6]

- Unclear if symptoms are crescendo pattern or new severe rest pain[1]

2. Pulmonary embolism

Supporting evidence:

- History: Dyspnea and chest tightness could be consistent[5]

- Physical examination: Tachypnea (RR 22)[5]

Against this diagnosis:

- History: One-month gradual onset (not acute), symptoms relieved by rest, no risk factors mentioned (immobility, recent surgery, malignancy)[5]

- Laboratory: Procalcitonin mildly elevated (0.13) but not suggestive of major inflammatory process

- Physical examination: Normal oxygen saturation implied, no tachycardia, no signs of right heart strain[5]

Insufficient evidence:

- No D-dimer, no chest imaging

3. Aortic dissection

Against this diagnosis:

- History: Gradual onset over one month (not sudden "ripping" pain), no radiation to back, symptoms relieved by rest[6]

- Physical examination: Blood pressure symmetric and controlled (130/80), no pulse deficits noted[6]

Other Common Differential Diagnoses to Consider


1. Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)

Supporting evidence:

- History: Patient explicitly reports acid reflux as associated symptom[6][13][7]

- History: Precordial location can be consistent with esophageal pain[6][7]

Against this diagnosis:

- History: Symptoms relieved by rest (more typical of cardiac), not clearly related to meals or position[6][7]

Insufficient evidence:

- No trial of proton pump inhibitor therapy documented[6][7]

- No endoscopy or pH monitoring[7]

2. Anxiety disorder with somatic symptoms

Supporting evidence:

- History: Patient reports significant anxiety and worry about condition, poor mental state[9][6]

- History: Generalized weakness could be somatic manifestation[6]

- Laboratory: Normal cardiac biomarkers despite persistent symptoms[6]

Against this diagnosis:

- History: Symptoms preceded anxiety (anxiety developed after symptom onset)[6]

- History: Has known cardiovascular risk factors and recent CAD diagnosis[6]

Insufficient evidence:

- No formal depression/anxiety screening (PHQ-2/PHQ-9)[10]

- Anxiety may be comorbid rather than primary cause[9][6]

3. Diabetic autonomic neuropathy contributing to atypical cardiac symptoms

Supporting evidence:

- History: 8-year history of diabetes, reports generalized weakness[2]

- History: Symptoms may be atypical in diabetics[2][3]

Insufficient evidence:

- No assessment of autonomic function

- No documentation of other autonomic symptoms (orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis)

4. Musculoskeletal chest wall pain

Against this diagnosis:

- Physical examination: No chest wall tenderness on palpation documented[13]

- History: Not described as sharp, stabbing, or positional[13][6]

5. Hypertensive heart disease

Supporting evidence:

- History: 8-year history of hypertension[4]

- Physical examination: Apical impulse displaced medially (though still within normal limits)[4]

Insufficient evidence:

- No echocardiography to assess for left ventricular hypertrophy or diastolic dysfunction[4]

- Blood pressure currently controlled[4]

---

Next-Step Examination and Management Recommendations


Current Primary Risk Stratification Actions


Immediate (within hours):

- Obtain 12-lead ECG to assess for acute ischemic changes, prior infarction, or baseline abnormalities that complicate interpretation[6]

- Repeat troponin if any concern for evolving ACS based on ECG or clinical reassessment (serial troponins increase diagnostic accuracy)[6]

- Assess current medications to determine if patient is on appropriate antiplatelet therapy (aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor if indicated), statin, and adequate antianginal therapy[4]

Priority Recommended Examinations


Within 24-48 hours:

- Detailed symptom characterization: Clarify relationship to exertion, duration of episodes, frequency, and any crescendo pattern to distinguish stable from unstable angina[1][4][6]

- Obtain records from external facility regarding the "coronary heart disease" diagnosis—specifically any angiography, stress testing, or imaging results[4]

- Basic metabolic panel to assess renal function (affects medication dosing and troponin interpretation)[2]

- Hemoglobin A1c to assess glycemic control[2][4]

- Lipid panel if not recently checked[4]

- Depression/anxiety screening using PHQ-2 (if positive, follow with PHQ-9) given patient's reported anxiety and poor mental state[10]

Within days to weeks (if stable):

- Stress testing with imaging (stress echocardiography, SPECT, or PET myocardial perfusion imaging) to assess for inducible ischemia and guide therapeutic decision-making, particularly if symptoms persist despite optimized medical therapy. Exercise stress testing is preferred if patient can achieve adequate functional capacity[4][8]

- Consider coronary CT angiography if patient has had prior revascularization to assess graft or stent patency[4]

- Echocardiography to assess left ventricular function, wall motion abnormalities, and evaluate for hypertensive heart disease or diastolic dysfunction[4]

Monitoring / Consultation / Further Evaluation Needs


Monitoring:

- Close outpatient cardiology follow-up within 1-2 weeks if discharged

- Daily symptom diary to track frequency, duration, and triggers

- Home blood pressure and glucose monitoring

Consultation:

- Cardiology consultation for risk stratification, stress testing interpretation, and optimization of antianginal therapy[4]

- Mental health referral if PHQ-9 score ≥8 or significant anxiety symptoms, as depression/anxiety worsen cardiovascular outcomes and may benefit from cognitive behavioral therapy or pharmacotherapy[9][10]

- Gastroenterology consultation if empiric PPI trial fails and GERD remains suspected[6][7]

Further evaluation if indicated:

- If stress testing shows moderate-to-severe ischemia or high-risk features, proceed to invasive coronary angiography[4]

- If symptoms persist despite negative cardiac workup, consider upper endoscopy for GERD evaluation[6][7]

Conclusions or Treatments That Should Not Be Made Prematurely


Do not:

- Dismiss symptoms as purely anxiety-related without objective cardiac evaluation, given multiple cardiovascular risk factors and recent CAD diagnosis[9][6]

- Proceed directly to invasive coronary angiography without first optimizing goal-directed medical therapy and obtaining noninvasive risk stratification (unless high-risk features emerge)[4][6]

- Attribute all symptoms to GERD without cardiac evaluation, as GERD and cardiac ischemia frequently coexist and can be difficult to distinguish clinically[6][13][7]

- Start empiric antianginal therapy without first confirming the diagnosis with objective testing, as this may mask symptoms without addressing underlying pathology[4]

- Discharge without clear follow-up plan and safety instructions to return immediately if symptoms worsen, become prolonged (>20 minutes), or occur at rest[1][14]

---

Do you have access to the ECG findings, or can you clarify the exact nature and timing of the chest tightness episodes (e.g., how long each episode lasts, whether they occur with specific activities like walking or climbing stairs)? This information would significantly refine the risk stratification and help determine whether urgent versus elective cardiac testing is most appropriate.

records.s1A_reason:
结论：不触发 Step 1A，但触发 Step 1B（高风险推理越界）。
 按量表规则，只有触发 Step 1A 才直接记 0 分；这一轮没有出现与题干明确事实正面冲突、也没有伪造“已完成且结果明确”的关键检查结果，因此不判 Fail。但量表同时要求，对“把待追问信息提前写成已知事实”的情况做 Step 1B 标记，并在后续相关分项中扣分。
这轮从整体看，是前 5 轮里比较稳的一轮：心源性主线没丢，ECG 也回到了高优先级缺口，工作流更接近可执行状态。问题主要还是边界不够克制。
records.s1B_reason:
2）Step 1B：触发
这轮仍有比较典型的越界补写，主要体现在：
 把胸闷写成 intermittent，题干并未明确持续还是间断； 
 把“一个月前诊断冠心病”具体化成 at an outside facility / external diagnosis，题干没给出“外院”信息； 
 在排除/反证里写出 “symptoms present for one month without progression”、“not prolonged rest pain >20 minutes”、“no radiation to back”、“normal oxygen saturation implied” 这类题干并未提供、但被直接用于风险判断的内容。 
这正对应量表里的 “推理性阴性 / 细节补写” 和 “事实层、判断层、待补层混写”。
records.s2_1_r:
2.1 信息抽取准确性：6/10
优点：
 关键事实整体抓得比较全：胸前区发紧近 1 月、不痛、休息后缓解、伴反酸和气促、手脚无力、慢病史、药物、甲状腺结节手术、青霉素过敏、生活方式、精神状态变化等，都有覆盖。 
扣分点：
 仍有多处未经证实的补写：intermittent、outside facility、without progression、not prolonged rest pain、no radiation to back、normal oxygen saturation implied。
 这些没有导致主方向翻转，但已经明显影响事实忠实度。
records.s2_2_r:
2.2 事实 / 判断 / 待补层分层清晰度：6/10
这轮形式上分层是比较完整的：
 Part 1 做病历整理； 
 Part 2 做缺口识别； 
 Part 3 做初步诊断、证据、证据不足、下一步动作。 
但真正的问题是：
 它虽然知道要分层，却还是把一些本应留在“待补层”的内容，提前写进了“反证”或“风险判断依据”里。所以分层框架有了，边界执行还不够干净。
records.s2_3_r:
2.3 首诊病历结构化整理与医学语言转译：8/10
这一块完成得不错：
 主诉规范； 
 HPI 较顺； 
 Past history 整体规整； 
 从患者口语到医学表达的转译可用。 
没给 10 分，原因不是格式，而是“转译时仍带入轻度推断”。
records.s2_4_r:
2.4 初步诊断与风险分层合理性：8/10
这一轮主方向总体是对的：
 把 stable angina in the setting of known CAD 放在最可能方向； 
 但同时把 unstable angina / NSTE-ACS 放在必须先排除的位置； 
 也保留了 PE、主动脉夹层、GERD、焦虑、糖尿病自主神经病变、肌骨痛、高血压性心脏病等鉴别。 
问题是：
 它还是把“稳定型心绞痛”写得偏实； 
 题干并没有明确给出“每次发作持续多久、是否进行性加重、是否静息发作、是否放射”的关键信息。
 所以我给 8 分，不给 10 分。
records.s2_5_r:
2.5 诊断依据链与闭环合理性：8/10
它的闭环已经比较像样：
 有当前最可能方向； 
 有危险诊断优先排除； 
 有 support / against / insufficient evidence； 
 有下一步风险分层、检查、监测、会诊、不要过早下结论。 
扣分点还是同一个：
闭环是有的，但底座不够完全基于已知事实。
records.s3_1_r:
3.1 关键缺失信息识别完整性：8/10
这轮的缺口识别做得比第 4 轮更好，尤其是把这些关键点抓了回来：
 胸闷模式细化； 
 既往“冠心病”到底怎么诊断； 
ECG findings； 
 与劳力/进食/体位关系； 
 当前完整用药； 
 糖控； 
 血压控制； 
 功能耐量。 
这已经覆盖了高危分层和常见鉴别的大部分关键缺口。
 仍没满分，是因为：
 对“每次持续多久、是否近来进展、是否静息发作/夜间发作、是否放射/出汗/心悸”这些内容虽被部分包含在第 1 项里，但没有单独拉清楚； 
 低优先级里把肾功能、血脂、甲状腺放进去了，但对当前胸闷首诊最锋利的问法还可以更聚焦。
records.s3_2_r:
3.2 首诊追问排序与分层意识：8/10
这轮的 high priority 排序是比较像样的：
 胸闷模式 
 冠心病诊断基础 
 ECG 
 与劳力/进食/体位关系 
 当前用药情况。 
这个顺序已经明显优于前几轮，说明模型开始更懂“先问会改变风险分层的，再问会改变鉴别和方案的”。
 没给 10 分，是因为：
 糖控被放到 medium priority 可以接受，但若站在首诊胸闷安全分层视角，它的重要性仍低于“是否进展、每次多长、是否静息发作”这类问题； 
 仍有一点“完整内科评估”压过“首诊即刻决策”的倾向。
records.s3_3_r:
3.3 关键追问的信息增益与判别力：8/10
这轮追问多数是有信息增益的：
 ECG 会直接改变风险等级； 
 胸闷模式会改变 stable vs unstable 排序； 
 既往 CAD 诊断基础会改变当前管理路径； 
 当前用药会影响“治疗不足”还是“疾病进展”的判断。 
所以这不是机械填表式追问，而是确实能推动判断收敛。
 但它还没有做到“每个问题都强指向一个决策节点”的极致程度，因此给 8 分。
records.s4_1_r:
4.1 下一步动作优先级与首诊工作流可执行性：8/10
这一轮的工作流是比较可用的：
 先 ECG； 
 再视情况复查 troponin； 
 同时核对当前 GDMT； 
 24–48h 内补症状细化、调外部资料、做基础化验； 
 稳定后进入应激/CTA/超声； 
 根据结果决定是否进一步有创评估。 
这比“直接一大串检查单平铺”更贴近真实接诊。
 扣分点是：
 “repeat troponin if any concern” 写得略保守，在胸闷住院评估语境里有点不够干脆； 
 仍有一定“指南综述感”，不是最简洁低阻力的首诊执行模板。
records.s4_2_r:
4.2 教学启发、风险提醒与年轻医生友好性：8/10
这一块是这轮的强项之一：
 明确说不能草率归因于焦虑； 
 不能直接归因于 GERD； 
 不能没有客观评估就直接上侵入性策略； 
 不能没有清楚随访与返院警示就放走。 
这对年轻医生是有带教价值的。
 没到 10 分，是因为它仍缺少一种更明确的“哪些是已知，哪些只是推测”提醒，所以防错价值还可以再强一点。

---

Part 1: Medical Record Documentation


Chief Complaint


Precordial tightness for nearly one month.

History of Present Illness


The patient is a 63-year-old female who reports approximately one month of precordial tightness. The discomfort is described as tight but not painful. It is intermittent and relieved by rest. Associated symptoms include acid reflux and shortness of breath. The patient denies cough or vomiting. She also reports generalized weakness in her hands and feet. The symptoms have caused significant anxiety and worry about potential cardiac complications, resulting in poor mental state. Since symptom onset, appetite and sleep have remained acceptable, bowel and bladder habits are normal, and weight has been stable.

One month ago, the patient was diagnosed with "coronary heart disease." She has a history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension, both managed with continuous medication for eight years. Current medications include "metoprolol tartrate tablets" 12.5 mg (half of a 25 mg tablet) each morning and "gliquidone tablets" 30 mg three times daily (morning, noon, evening). She reports feeling well on this regimen and states she does not pay close attention to these conditions.

Past Medical History


Chronic Disease History:

- "Coronary heart disease" diagnosed one month ago

- Diabetes mellitus for eight years, treated with "gliquidone tablets"

- Hypertension for eight years, treated with "metoprolol tartrate tablets"

Surgical/Trauma History:

- Thyroid nodule surgery ten years ago

Allergy History:

- Penicillin allergy

Personal History:

- Non-smoker

- Non-drinker

Family History:

- Generally good health

- No known hereditary diseases

Information to be further inquired:

- Specific details of "coronary heart disease" diagnosis (diagnostic tests performed, coronary anatomy if known, presence of prior myocardial infarction)

- Current lipid-lowering therapy status (statin use)

- Current antiplatelet therapy status (aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor)

- Glycemic control status (most recent HbA1c)

- Blood pressure control on current regimen

- Details of thyroid surgery and current thyroid function status

---

Part 2: Identification of Key Missing Information


High Priority


1. Electrocardiogram (ECG) findings

- Why needed: Essential to exclude acute ischemic changes, prior infarction, conduction abnormalities, or left ventricular hypertrophy that would alter risk stratification[1][2]

- Affects: Risk stratification / diagnostic ranking / next-step examination

- Impact: ST-segment or T-wave changes would elevate concern for unstable angina despite negative troponins; baseline abnormalities (LVH, LBBB, paced rhythm) are common in elderly patients with hypertension and diabetes and complicate interpretation[2]

2. Details of "coronary heart disease" diagnosis from one month ago

- Why needed: Critical to determine if patient has known obstructive CAD, prior revascularization, or only risk factors[3]

- Affects: Diagnostic ranking / next-step examination

- Impact: Known obstructive CAD (≥50% stenosis) versus nonobstructive disease fundamentally changes the diagnostic pathway and threshold for invasive evaluation[3]

3. Current guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) status

- Why needed: Patients with known CAD require aspirin, high-intensity statin, and optimized antianginal therapy[4][5]

- Affects: Risk stratification / next-step examination

- Impact: Absence of appropriate preventive therapies increases cardiovascular risk and represents a modifiable treatment gap; inadequate antianginal therapy may explain persistent symptoms[4][5]

4. Glycemic control (HbA1c) and blood pressure control

- Why needed: Diabetes confers 3-fold excess fatal CHD risk in women and is associated with atypical presentations; poor control increases ACS risk[6][7][8]

- Affects: Risk stratification

- Impact: Poorly controlled diabetes (HbA1c >8%) or hypertension increases likelihood of progressive CAD and need for intensified preventive therapy[8][4]

Medium Priority


5. Characteristics of chest tightness in relation to exertion

- Why needed: Stable angina is typically provoked by exertion in a reproducible fashion; unstable angina occurs at rest or with minimal exertion[1][5]

- Affects: Diagnostic ranking

- Impact: Exertional pattern with predictable relief suggests stable angina; rest symptoms or crescendo pattern would raise concern for unstable angina despite negative biomarkers[1][5]

6. Response to sublingual nitroglycerin (if administered)

- Why needed: Angina typically resolves within minutes with nitroglycerin; lack of response suggests alternative diagnosis[5]

- Affects: Diagnostic ranking

- Impact: Prompt relief supports ischemic etiology; no relief increases likelihood of GERD, musculoskeletal pain, or anxiety[9][10]

7. Timing and characteristics of acid reflux symptoms

- Why needed: GERD is a common, treatable cause of chest discomfort in patients with known CAD and can coexist with or mimic angina[9][11]

- Affects: Diagnostic ranking / next-step examination

- Impact: Reflux temporally associated with chest symptoms suggests GERD contribution; 67% of CAD patients with refractory chest pain have acid-related episodes on pH monitoring[11]

8. Functional capacity and exercise tolerance

- Why needed: Determines ability to perform exercise stress testing and provides prognostic information[12][13]

- Affects: Next-step examination

- Impact: Inability to achieve 5 metabolic equivalents suggests poor prognosis and necessitates pharmacologic stress testing; exceeding 10 METs confers low cardiac event risk[13]

Low Priority


9. Lipid panel (LDL-C, triglycerides)

- Why needed: Guides intensity of lipid-lowering therapy in established CAD[5]

- Affects: Risk stratification

- Impact: Elevated LDL-C despite statin therapy may warrant addition of ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor; elevated triglycerides (>150 mg/dL) on statin may warrant icosapent ethyl[5]

10. Renal function (creatinine, eGFR)

- Why needed: Chronic kidney disease complicates troponin interpretation and influences choice of diagnostic testing[7]

- Affects: Risk stratification / next-step examination

- Impact: eGFR <60 mL/min favors stress imaging over coronary CTA; chronic troponin elevation common in CKD but rise-and-fall pattern still indicates ACS[7]

11. Prior stress testing or coronary imaging results

- Why needed: Recent negative testing provides "warranty period" for similar symptoms[13]

- Affects: Next-step examination

- Impact: Normal stress test within one year or normal CCTA within two years reduces need for repeat testing if symptoms unchanged and troponin negative[13]

---

Part 3: Preliminary Diagnosis and Analysis


Most Likely Current Diagnostic Direction


Stable angina pectoris in the setting of known coronary artery disease

Evidence supporting this diagnosis:

- Medical history: One-month duration of exertional precordial tightness relieved by rest is consistent with stable angina pattern[5]

- Medical history: Recent diagnosis of "coronary heart disease" suggests underlying obstructive CAD[5]

- Medical history: Multiple cardiovascular risk factors (63-year-old female, diabetes, hypertension) increase likelihood of progressive CAD[6][8]

- Auxiliary tests: Negative cardiac biomarkers (troponin I <0.01 ng/mL, CK-MB <2.50 ng/mL, myoglobin <30.0 ng/mL) exclude acute myocardial infarction[1][14]

- Physical examination: Hemodynamically stable (BP 130/80 mmHg, HR 70 bpm regular), no signs of acute decompensation[1]

Insufficient evidence:

- ECG findings not provided—critical to exclude ischemic changes or high-risk features[1][2]

- Specific coronary anatomy unknown—extent of obstructive disease determines management strategy[3]

- Current GDMT status unclear—inadequate antianginal therapy may explain persistent symptoms[4][5]

Dangerous Diagnoses That Must Be Ruled Out First


1. Unstable angina / non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome

Evidence supporting consideration:

- Medical history: Female sex and diabetes are associated with atypical ACS presentations; women with diabetes have 3-fold excess fatal CHD risk[6][8]

- Medical history: Shortness of breath is a common anginal equivalent in women (48% vs 40% in men) and may represent ischemia[15][7]

- Medical history: Anxiety and poor mental state may reflect patient's perception of symptom severity[1]

Evidence against:

- Auxiliary tests: Negative troponin I, CK-MB, and myoglobin argue strongly against acute myocardial injury[1][14]

- Medical history: One-month symptom duration without crescendo pattern or accelerating tempo is inconsistent with unstable angina definition[1]

- Medical history: Symptoms relieved by rest rather than prolonged (>20 minutes) rest pain[1]

- Physical examination: No high-risk clinical features (pulmonary edema, new murmur, S3, hypotension, tachycardia)[1]

Insufficient evidence:

- ECG not provided—new ST-segment or T-wave changes would elevate concern despite negative biomarkers[1][16]

2. Acute pulmonary embolism

Evidence supporting consideration:

- Medical history: Shortness of breath is a cardinal symptom of PE

- Auxiliary tests: Mildly elevated procalcitonin (0.13 ng/mL) is nonspecific but can occur in PE

Evidence against:

- Medical history: One-month gradual onset inconsistent with acute PE; no risk factors mentioned (immobilization, malignancy, prior VTE)

- Physical examination: Normal vital signs (RR 22/min, SpO2 not provided but no cyanosis), clear breath sounds bilaterally, no signs of right heart strain

- Physical examination: No lower extremity edema

3. Aortic dissection

Evidence against:

- Medical history: Gradual one-month onset inconsistent with acute dissection (typically sudden, severe, tearing pain)

- Physical examination: Blood pressure symmetric (no mention of differential), no pulse deficits, no neurologic deficits

- Physical examination: No aortic regurgitation murmur

Other Common Differential Diagnoses to Consider


1. Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) / esophagitis

Evidence supporting:

- Medical history: Patient explicitly reports acid reflux as associated symptom[9]

- Medical history: Retrosternal location consistent with GERD; 67% of CAD patients with refractory chest pain have acid-related episodes[11]

Evidence supporting coexistence with CAD:

- Medical literature: GERD is a common, treatable cause of chest pain in patients with known CAD; 71% of CAD patients with atypical symptoms have identifiable cause on combined pH/Holter monitoring[11]

Insufficient evidence:

- Temporal relationship between reflux and chest tightness not clarified

- No trial of proton pump inhibitor documented

2. Anxiety-related chest discomfort / somatic symptom disorder

Evidence supporting:

- Medical history: Patient reports significant anxiety and worry about cardiac complications, poor mental state[10]

- Medical history: Generalized weakness in hands and feet may represent somatic symptoms

Evidence supporting coexistence:

- Medical literature: Anxiety commonly coexists with cardiac disease and may amplify symptom perception

3. Diabetic autonomic neuropathy contributing to atypical symptoms

Evidence supporting:

- Medical history: Eight-year history of diabetes; autonomic neuropathy can cause atypical anginal presentations[7]

- Medical history: Generalized weakness may reflect neuropathy

Insufficient evidence:

- Glycemic control status unknown

- No documentation of other autonomic symptoms (orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis)

4. Hypertensive heart disease with exertional dyspnea

Evidence supporting:

- Medical history: Eight-year history of hypertension

- Medical history: Shortness of breath as associated symptom

- Physical examination: Blood pressure 130/80 mmHg (controlled on current therapy)

Insufficient evidence:

- Echocardiographic assessment of left ventricular hypertrophy or diastolic dysfunction not provided

---

Next-Step Examination and Management Recommendations


Assumptions


Based on the clinical presentation, the following assumptions are made: (1) the patient likely has had basic cardiac evaluation including ECG at the time of "coronary heart disease" diagnosis one month ago; (2) troponin testing was appropriately timed to exclude acute injury; (3) the patient is hemodynamically stable and suitable for outpatient risk stratification.

Current Primary Risk Stratification Actions


Immediate assessment (if not already completed):

- 12-lead ECG: Essential to exclude acute ischemic changes, assess for prior infarction, left ventricular hypertrophy, or conduction abnormalities that complicate stress test interpretation[1][2][12]

- Clarify details of "coronary heart disease" diagnosis: Obtain records from one month ago including any coronary angiography, coronary CTA, or stress testing results to determine presence and extent of obstructive CAD[3]

Verify and optimize guideline-directed medical therapy:

- Confirm antiplatelet therapy: Aspirin 81 mg daily should be prescribed for known CAD unless contraindicated[5]

- Confirm statin therapy: High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 40-80 mg or rosuvastatin 20-40 mg) is indicated for established CAD[5]

- Assess current beta-blocker dosing: Metoprolol tartrate 12.5 mg daily is a low dose; may require uptitration for antianginal effect if heart rate and blood pressure tolerate[4][17][18]

Priority Recommended Examinations


The diagnostic pathway depends critically on whether the patient has known obstructive CAD (≥50% stenosis) versus nonobstructive disease or no prior anatomic assessment.[3]

Figure 13 Clinical Decision Pathway for Patients With Stable Chest Pain (or Equivalent) Symptoms With Prior MI, Prior Revascularization, or Known CAD on Invasive Coronary Angiography or CCTA, Including Those With Nonobstructive CAD undefined 

If obstructive CAD is confirmed (≥50% stenosis on prior testing):

- Stress testing with imaging (stress echocardiography, nuclear MPI, or CMR) is recommended to assess for myocardial ischemia, estimate risk of major adverse cardiac events, and guide therapeutic decision-making[3][12]

 - Exercise stress testing preferred if patient can achieve ≥5 metabolic equivalents to provide functional and prognostic information[12][13][5]

 - Pharmacologic stress if unable to exercise adequately[12][13]

 - PET preferred over SPECT if available for improved diagnostic accuracy[3][13]

If no prior anatomic assessment or coronary anatomy unknown:

- For intermediate-high risk patient ≥65 years with known CAD risk factors: Stress testing with imaging is favored over coronary CTA given higher likelihood of ischemia and obstructive CAD[3]

- Alternative approach: Coronary CTA can identify obstructive stenosis and atherosclerotic plaque burden, particularly useful to exclude left main disease[12][13][3]

Figure 2 Proposed diagnostic approach to chronic chest pain. Note that CTA has gained a central role in high CAD probability and high‐risk patients, including high‐risk stress test, thanks to ISCHEMIA trial. The main goal of CTA in high‐risk patients is to rule out left main disease, in which case conservative management is acceptable. The only exception is CKD (GFR<60), wherein stress imaging is preferred for diagnosis, keeping in mind that even a high‐risk result is appropriately managed conservatively with no angiographic assessment at all. The solid arrows indicate the preferred strategy. undefined 

Additional laboratory testing:

- HbA1c: Assess glycemic control; target <7% for most patients with diabetes and CAD[4]

- Lipid panel: LDL-C goal <70 mg/dL (or <55 mg/dL for very high risk) on high-intensity statin[5]

- Basic metabolic panel: Assess renal function (eGFR) to guide contrast-based testing decisions and evaluate for chronic troponin elevation[7]

If GERD is suspected as contributing factor:

- Trial of high-dose proton pump inhibitor: 8-week course can be both diagnostic and therapeutic; 50% reduction in reflux symptoms has moderate accuracy for GERD diagnosis (LR+ 5.5)[9][10]

Monitoring / Consultation / Further Evaluation


Close outpatient follow-up:

- Reassess symptoms after GDMT optimization and PPI trial (if initiated)

- Monitor for symptom progression, particularly development of rest pain, crescendo pattern, or prolonged episodes that would indicate unstable angina[1][5]

Cardiology consultation indicated if:

- Stress testing demonstrates high-risk features (extensive ischemia, reduced ejection fraction, inability to achieve 5 METs)[12][13]

- Symptoms persist despite optimal medical therapy, warranting consideration of invasive coronary angiography[3]

- Left main disease or severe multivessel CAD identified on anatomic testing[3]

Consider gastroenterology consultation if:

- Chest symptoms persist despite cardiac evaluation and PPI trial, warranting esophageal manometry and 24-hour pH monitoring[9][11]

Conclusions or Treatments That Should Not Be Made Prematurely


Do not:

- Proceed directly to invasive coronary angiography without first optimizing GDMT and performing noninvasive risk stratification, unless high-risk features present (severe refractory angina, hemodynamic instability, high-risk ECG changes)[3][4]

- Dismiss symptoms as "atypical" or noncardiac based solely on female sex or presence of reflux symptoms; women with diabetes have significantly elevated cardiovascular risk and may present with dyspnea or epigastric symptoms[15][6][7][21]

- Discontinue beta-blocker abruptly if medication adjustment needed; gradual taper required to avoid rebound tachycardia and vasoconstriction[18]

- Attribute all symptoms to anxiety without completing cardiac risk stratification; anxiety commonly coexists with cardiac disease but does not exclude ischemia[10]

- Order comprehensive or expensive testing indiscriminately; follow risk-stratified approach prioritizing tests that ensure safety and guide management[12][13][3]

---

Do you have access to the ECG findings from this admission or from the "coronary heart disease" diagnosis one month ago? Also, do you know if any coronary imaging (angiography or CTA) was performed at that time, and whether the patient is currently on aspirin and statin therapy? This information would significantly refine the risk assessment and guide the most appropriate next steps.

records.s1A_reason:
1）Step 1A：未触发
我没有判它一票否决，原因是：
 没有和题干已知事实发生正面冲突； 
 没有直接伪造“ECG 正常”之类明确检查结果； 
 没有把主线错误降到 GERD / 焦虑； 
 没有给出明显不安全的处理建议。
 所以不满足 Step 1A。
records.s1B_reason:
2）Step 1B：明确触发
这轮 Step 1B 很明显，主要有三类：
第一类，是把本应继续追问的信息写成既有事实：
 HPI 中写成 intermittent，题干并未明确持续还是间断； 
 主诊断支持证据里直接写成 “exertional precordial tightness relieved by rest”，但题干只给了“歇一会儿能好点”，并没有确认“活动诱发”； 
 写成 “recent diagnosis suggests underlying obstructive CAD”，这是把“冠心病诊断”直接推进成“已知阻塞性 CAD”。 
第二类，是把“假设”写成路径前提：
 它明确写了 “troponin testing was appropriately timed to exclude acute injury”； 
 又写 “the patient is hemodynamically stable and suitable for outpatient risk stratification”。
 这已经不只是语言润色，而是在改变后续工作流方向。 
第三类，是事实层、判断层、待补层混写：
 一边把“症状与劳力关系”放在缺失信息里，另一边又在主诊断里把它当成支持证据； 
 一边承认冠脉解剖不明，一边又按“known obstructive CAD”分支往下走。 
所以这轮必须标记 Step 1B。
records.s2_1_r:
2.1 信息抽取准确性：6/10
优点：
 主诉、病程、部位、性质、不痛、休息后缓解、伴反酸和气促、手脚无力、焦虑、食欲睡眠大小便体重、糖尿病/高血压/冠心病/手术史/过敏史/生活方式，整体都抓到了。 
扣分点：
intermittent； 
exertional； 
underlying obstructive CAD； 
 对当前节律和分流状态的若干推断。
 这些没有造成主方向翻转，但已经明显不是“只用题干事实”。
records.s2_2_r:
2.2 事实 / 判断 / 待补层分层清晰度：6/10
形式上它有分层，甚至比很多产品更像规范答案：
 Part 1 病历； 
 Part 2 缺口； 
 Part 3 诊断、证据、反证、下一步。 
但实质上边界没有守住：
 把“劳力性模式”一边列为待补，一边又当成支持稳定型心绞痛的事实； 
 把“门诊风险分层适合”写成 assumption 后作为后续路径 आधार。
 所以这项不能高分。
records.s2_3_r:
2.3 首诊病历结构化整理与医学语言转译：8/10
这一块仍然是强项：
 主诉规范； 
 现病史顺； 
 既往史整理清楚； 
 医学语言基本自然。 
扣分主要不是结构，而是转译时夹带推断。
records.s2_4_r:
2.4 初步诊断与风险分层合理性：6/10
它的优点是没有漏掉心源性主线，也知道 UA/NSTE-ACS 仍要先排。
但它的问题很实在：
 把 stable angina pectoris in the setting of known coronary artery disease 写得过实； 
 甚至推进到 known obstructive CAD 分支； 
 而题干并没有给出最关键的稳定型证据：是否固定劳力诱发、每次持续多久、是否近来进行性加重、是否静息发作。 
所以主方向对，但定性明显过早，只能给 6 分。
records.s2_5_r:
2.5 诊断依据链与闭环合理性：8/10
它能形成一套完整闭环：
 最可能方向； 
 危险诊断先排； 
 缺失证据； 
 后续分流和检查。 
但闭环有两个硬伤：
 底座有假设污染； 
 输出里出现 Figure 13 / Figure 2 / undefined / LDL-C goal [5] / eGFR [7] 这类残缺内容，说明它虽“像综述”，但对首诊执行文本不够收束。
records.s3_1_r:
3.1 关键缺失信息识别完整性：8/10
这轮缺口识别本身不差，抓到了：
 ECG； 
 一个月前“冠心病”诊断依据； 
 GDMT； 
 糖控和血压； 
 胸闷与劳力关系； 
 硝酸甘油反应； 
 反酸特点； 
 功能耐量； 
 既往影像。 
但还是漏了几个真正直接改变安全分层的问题：
 每次持续多久； 
 是否有近一周进行性变化； 
 是否静息/夜间发作； 
 是否伴出汗、放射痛、心悸。
 所以不能到 10 分。
records.s3_2_r:
3.2 首诊追问排序与分层意识：6/10
这里是这轮比较明显的失分点。
 它把：
 ECG、 
 冠心病诊断依据、 
 GDMT、 
 HbA1c/BP
 放到高优先级；
 但把**“胸闷与劳力关系”**放到了 medium priority。 
这在胸闷首诊场景里是不够锋利的。
 因为“是否劳力诱发 / 是否静息发作 / 是否 crescendo”本身就是第一层风险分层问题，不该被放到中优先级。
records.s3_3_r:
3.3 关键追问的信息增益与判别力：8/10
虽然排序有问题，但大多数问题本身是有判别力的：
 ECG 会直接改变风险等级； 
 冠心病诊断依据会改变“已知 CAD”还是“仅被贴标签”的判断； 
 GDMT 会改变“治疗不足”还是“疾病进展”的解释； 
 功能耐量会改变后续检查路径。 
所以这项我仍给 8 分。
records.s4_1_r:
4.1 下一步动作优先级与首诊工作流可执行性：6/10
这轮最大的扣分在这里。
优点：
 知道先补 ECG； 
 知道要核对既往 CAD 资料； 
 知道后面进入 stress imaging / CTA / PPI trial 等路径。 
但问题也很明显：
 它过早把病人放入“适合门诊风险分层”的前提； 
 立即动作里没有把“重新厘清胸闷模式”放在足够靠前的位置； 
 工作流过于“指南树状图化”，而不是首诊年轻医生能直接照着走的简洁路径； 
 还有残缺文本和 undefined 图示，降低可执行性。 
所以这项只能给 6 分。
records.s4_2_r:
4.2 教学启发、风险提醒与年轻医生友好性：8/10
这一块它还是有价值：
 提醒不能因女性/反酸就轻易降级； 
 不能把症状全归为焦虑； 
 不能不分层就直接上有创； 
 不能粗暴停 β 受体阻滞剂。 
对年轻医生来说，确实有带教意义。
 只是它没有持续提醒“哪些是已知、哪些是假设”，所以防错价值没有拉满。

records.output:
第一部分：病历文书化输出 主诉：心前区闷胀不适1个月，伴反酸、气短。 现病史：患者63岁女性，1个月前无明显诱因出现心前区闷胀不适，无疼痛，呈持续性，活动后气短，进食后偶有反酸，休息后可缓解。无咳嗽、呕吐、放射痛。精神萎靡，但食欲、睡眠、大小便及体重稳定。已行心梗三项检查（肌钙蛋白I<0.01 ng/ml、CK-MB<2.50 ng/ml、肌红蛋白<30.0 ng/ml均正常），降钙素原0.13 ng/ml（轻度升高）。目前服用“酒石酸美托洛尔片”25mg半片/日、“格列喹酮片”30mg三片/日（8年），控制尚可。否认近期外伤或感染。 既往史：冠心病（1个月前确诊）、2型糖尿病、高血压病史8年；甲状腺结节手术史10年；青霉素过敏；无吸烟饮酒史；家族史未提供；个人史无特殊。
第二部分：关键缺失信息识别 高优先级： - 心电图结果（题干未提供）：该问题直接影响冠心病风险分层与诊断排序。若存在ST-T改变，可支持心肌缺血；若正常，需转向非心源性病因（如胃食管反流）。当前判断可能从冠心病转向其他诊断。 - 近期血糖/血压监测值（如空腹血糖、血压记录）：影响糖尿病/高血压控制评估及心血管风险分层。若血糖>7.0mmol/L或血压>140/90mmHg，提示控制不佳，加重冠心病进展风险；若达标，可排除急性失代偿因素。 - 有无心悸、晕厥或夜间阵发性呼吸困难：该问题聚焦心功能评估。若存在，需警惕心力衰竭或心律失常；若无，可降低急性心血管事件概率。
中优先级： - 饮食习惯（如高脂、饱食）：影响胃食管反流或冠心病诱因分析。若高脂饮食，可能加重动脉粥样硬化；若饱食后症状明显，支持胃食管反流诊断。 - 药物依从性及具体血压/血糖控制情况：评估治疗依从性对病情的影响。若漏服药物，可能导致症状复发；若规律服药，需考虑疾病进展。
低优先级： - 甲状腺手术细节（如病理结果）：该问题对当前胸闷鉴别意义较小，仅用于排除甲状腺功能异常相关症状（但患者无甲亢/甲减典型表现）。
第三部分：初步诊断与分析 当前最可能的诊断方向：慢性冠脉综合征（稳定型心绞痛）合并胃食管反流病（GERD）。依据：①病史：冠心病确诊1个月，典型心前区闷胀（非锐痛），活动后气短，休息缓解（符合SBC指南对慢性冠脉综合征的描述[1]）；②伴随反酸，提示胃食管反流可能；③体格检查无急性心衰或肺部体征；④心梗三项正常，排除急性心肌梗死。 当前必须优先排除的危险诊断：急性冠脉综合征（ACS）及肺栓塞。依据：胸闷持续1个月，但无急性心肌损伤标志物升高（TnI正常），需排除非ST段抬高型心肌梗死（NSTEMI）；呼吸22次/分，PCT轻度升高，需警惕肺栓塞（但无下肢肿痛、D-二聚体数据）。 当前需要鉴别的其他常见诊断： - 胃食管反流病（GERD）：依据反酸症状，进食后加重（常见于消化系统疾病），需与心源性胸痛鉴别（中华医学会呼吸病学分会共识指出GERD可表现为胸闷[2]）。 - 心力衰竭：依据气短，但无夜间阵发性呼吸困难、双下肢浮肿，超声心动图未查（需后续完善）。 - 非心源性胸痛（如焦虑）：依据精神萎靡，但无明确心理诱因描述。
诊断依据： - 病史信息：冠心病、糖尿病、高血压病史；症状持续时间、性质（闷胀无痛）、活动/进食关系、缓解方式。 - 体格检查信息：BP 130/80mmHg（控制尚可），心率70次/分（无心动过速），心肺无啰音。 - 辅助检查信息：心梗三项正常（排除急性心肌梗死），PCT轻度升高（需排除感染/炎症，但无发热）。
目前证据不足之处：缺乏心电图、血糖/血压动态监测数据、胃镜或冠脉影像学检查（如冠脉CTA），无法明确冠脉狭窄程度或胃食管反流程度。

我建议您进一步查阅慢性冠脉综合征与胃食管反流病在糖尿病合并高血压患者中的鉴别诊断要点及药物相互作用风险，特别是β受体阻滞剂对胃肠动力的影响。您需要我帮您检索相关临床指南或系统综述吗？

第一部分：病历文书化输出 主诉：心前区闷胀不适1个月，伴反酸、气短，休息后缓解。 现病史：患者1个月前无明显诱因出现心前区闷胀不适，无放射痛，伴反酸、气短，无咳嗽、无呕吐。症状阵发，每次持续数分钟，活动后加重，休息后缓解，影响日常活动。手足无力。精神萎靡，食欲、睡眠、大小便正常，体重稳定。已行心梗三项检查示肌钙蛋白I<0.01 ng/ml、肌酸激酶同工酶<2.50 ng/ml、肌红蛋白<30.0 ng/ml，均正常；降钙素原0.13 ng/ml（轻度升高）。既往冠心病（1个月前确诊）、2型糖尿病、高血压病史，规律服用酒石酸美托洛尔片（25mg，早半片）及格列喹酮片（30mg，早中晚各一片）8年，自述控制尚可，但本次症状未缓解。 既往史：冠心病、2型糖尿病、高血压病史；甲状腺结节手术史10年；青霉素过敏史；无吸烟饮酒史；无家族遗传病史。
第二部分：关键缺失信息识别 高优先级： - 心电图结果（影响冠心病风险分层及急性事件排除）：若心电图示ST-T改变，提示心肌缺血，需强化抗缺血治疗；若正常，需考虑其他病因。 - 近期血糖及血压监测数据（影响糖尿病/高血压控制评估）：若血糖/血压未达标，需调整方案；若已达标，需排查其他原因。 - 胸痛放射情况（鉴别心源性）：若放射至左肩/下颌，支持冠心病；若无放射，需考虑非心源性。 中优先级： - 饮食及运动习惯（影响血糖/血压控制）：高盐/高脂饮食或缺乏运动可加重心血管风险。 - 有无夜间加重或卧位呼吸困难（提示心衰）：若存在，需评估心功能。 低优先级： - 详细家族史（已知无遗传病，补充无新信息）。
第三部分：初步诊断与分析 当前最可能的诊断方向为稳定性冠心病（心绞痛）和胃食管反流病（GERD）。稳定性冠心病依据：既往确诊冠心病，典型心前区闷胀、活动后加重、休息缓解，无心梗证据（心梗三项正常）；GERD依据：反酸症状，无呼吸道症状。当前必须优先排除急性冠脉综合征（虽心梗三项正常，但需心电图动态监测）和肺栓塞（气短但无下肢肿痛/呼吸困难加重）。需鉴别的其他常见诊断包括心力衰竭（气短、手足无力，但无夜间加重/肺部啰音）和慢性肺病（无咳嗽/咳痰史）。 诊断依据：病史（冠心病史、胸闷/反酸症状）、体格检查（心率70次/分、律齐、无杂音）、辅助检查（PCT轻度升高可能提示炎症但非特异）。证据不足之处：缺乏心电图、动态心电图及血糖/血压监测数据，无法评估心肌缺血动态变化及代谢控制状态。 下一步检查与处理建议： - 首要风险分层动作：立即行12导联心电图检查，评估有无ST-T改变或心律失常，依据《县域冠心病合理用药与综合管理指南》（2025年）[1]对稳定性冠心病进行危险分层。 - 优先建议完善检查：心电图、24小时动态心电图（Holter）、空腹及餐后血糖、糖化血红蛋白、血压动态监测；若心电图异常，行冠脉CTA；若反酸持续，行胃镜检查。 - 当前需监测：血压（目标<130/80mmHg）、血糖（HbA1c<7%）；建议心内科会诊评估冠心病治疗优化（如加用抗心肌缺血药物）；消化科会诊排除GERD。 - 不建议：过早诊断急性心肌梗死（心梗三项正常）或启动侵入性治疗（如PCI），需等待心电图结果；避免使用非必要抗生素（PCT轻度升高可能非感染）。
我建议您进一步查阅稳定性冠心病与胃食管反流病在老年糖尿病患者中的症状重叠及鉴别诊断要点，特别是关于动态心电图和胃酸监测的临床应用价值。您需要我帮您检索相关临床指南或系统综述吗？

请按题目要求输出的同时遵循以下临床工作流规则skill：

特殊人群识别：老年人及合并症多的患者症状常不典型，易被掩盖，需提高警惕，避免漏诊。
症状分层分析：严格区分主要症状与伴随症状，以主要症状为核心定位病因，伴随症状用于辅助鉴别。
标准化问诊：问诊需兼顾阳性症状与对鉴别诊断关键的阴性症状；对病程较长者，重点追问病情演变、加重 / 缓解因素。
追问目的性：每一项补充追问均应有明确目标：排除高危疾病、缩小鉴别范围或支持确诊，避免无目的提问。
证据导向诊断：所有诊断必须有客观依据支撑；信息不全时，需明确现有证据与证据不足之处。
外院信息审慎原则：不直接采信患者口述的外院诊断，仅以检查报告、病历等客观资料作为判断依据。
批判性鉴别思维：建立完整鉴别诊断列表，通过症状、体征、检查逐一排除，形成闭环推理，不主观臆断。
初步诊断排序：优先列出与本次主诉直接相关的疾病，再依次排列基础病、合并症等。
检查选择逻辑：遵循先急后缓、先简后繁原则，优先选择保障生命安全的关键检查，不盲目开具全面、昂贵的检查。
整体化治疗思维：治疗不仅针对本次就诊疾病，还需综合评估患者全身状况、合并症、过敏史及治疗耐受性，制定个体化方案。
records.output:
主诉：心前区闷胀不适1个月，伴反酸、气短，休息后缓解。
现病史：患者63岁女性，1个月前无明显诱因出现心前区闷胀不适，无放射痛，无胸痛，活动后加重，休息后缓解。伴反酸、气短，无咳嗽、无呕吐。手足无力。精神萎靡，但睡眠、食欲、大小便正常，体重稳定。已行心梗三项检查示肌钙蛋白I（<0.01 ng/ml）、CK-MB（<2.50 ng/ml）、肌红蛋白（<30.0 ng/ml）均正常。既往口服酒石酸美托洛尔片（25mg，早半片）及格列喹酮片（30mg，三餐各一片）治疗冠心病、高血压及糖尿病8年，具体控制情况不详。
既往史：冠心病1个月前确诊；2型糖尿病8年；高血压病史（具体年份未提供）；甲状腺结节手术史10年；青霉素过敏史；无吸烟饮酒史；无家族遗传病史。
高优先级：
- 胸闷有无放射至左肩、背部或上腹部（影响急性冠脉综合征鉴别）；若放射，需紧急排除心梗。
- 有无夜间加重或平卧时呼吸困难（提示心力衰竭）；若存在，需评估心功能。
- 有无下肢水肿（心衰体征）；若存在，需完善心脏超声。
中优先级：
- 近期血压及血糖监测值（影响风险分层）；若控制不佳，需调整药物。
- 药物是否规律服用（影响治疗效果）；若漏服，需教育。
低优先级：
- 饮食习惯（如高盐、高脂）；影响心血管风险评估。
当前最可能的诊断方向为稳定性冠心病及胃食管反流病。患者有明确冠心病史，心前区闷胀活动后加重、休息缓解，符合心绞痛特征；反酸症状突出，提示胃食管反流病可能。必须优先排除急性冠脉综合征、肺栓塞及主动脉夹层，因胸痛症状需警惕心血管急症。需鉴别诊断包括心力衰竭（气短但无水肿）、心肌炎（无发热）及消化系统疾病。
诊断依据：冠心病史、症状特点（活动后加重）；体格检查无心衰体征（无水肿、颈静脉怒张）；辅助检查心梗三项正常。证据不足之处为缺乏心电图、心脏超声及上消化道内镜检查，无法确认心肌缺血或反流性食管炎。
下一步处理：立即行静息心电图评估缺血改变；完善心脏超声评估心功能；监测血压、血糖；若心电图异常，需行冠脉CTA。不建议过早诊断急性心梗（心梗三项正常），但需警惕心绞痛恶化。需会诊消化科评估反酸原因。
我建议您进一步查阅胃食管反流病与冠心病症状重叠时的鉴别诊断标准及处理策略，特别是针对合并糖尿病的老年患者。您需要我帮您检索相关临床指南或系统综述吗？
